plan: Complete enhanced-ACT passage set: one original social science passage of about 640 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000030) on Hardin's tragedy of the commons and Elinor Ostrom's field research, with 9 questions (Key Ideas and Details 3, Craft and Structure 4, Integration 2). Facts kept to well-documented history (Hardin 1968; Ostrom's case studies including Swiss alpine pastures and Spanish irrigation; her design principles; Nobel Prize in economics 2009). Plus R030-10, a rebuilt replacement for R029-05 on passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000029 (already in the bank), restoring that passage's set to 9.

passages.title: Beyond the Tragedy
passages.text:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay with a memorable title, "The Tragedy of the Commons." Imagine, he wrote, a pasture open to every herder in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal to the pasture but bears only a small share of the damage that the extra grazing does. Reasoning this way, every herder adds animals, and the pasture is ruined. Hardin concluded that shared resources would be destroyed unless they were either divided into private property or placed under the control of a government.

The argument was elegant, and it spread quickly. It seemed to explain overfished seas, polluted rivers, and exhausted groundwater. For years many economists treated the tragedy less as a hypothesis to be tested than as a law to be applied.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom was not satisfied. Rather than reasoning about an imagined pasture, she went looking for real ones. With her colleagues, she gathered hundreds of case studies of fisheries, forests, irrigation systems, and grazing lands that communities had shared for long periods. In a Swiss mountain village, farmers had grazed cattle on common summer pastures for centuries under rules that limited how many animals each family could send up the mountain. In parts of Spain, farmers had shared water from irrigation canals for generations, taking turns according to schedules that everyone could see and that neighbors enforced on one another. Elected water judges heard complaints at regular public meetings, and a farmer caught taking water out of turn paid a fine set by people who knew the canal as well as the farmer did. Similar arrangements turned up in fishing villages, in forests held by villages in Japan, and in shared grazing lands elsewhere.

Ostrom did not claim that every commons succeeds. Many of her cases ended in collapse, just as Hardin predicted. Her point was that collapse is not inevitable. What distinguished the lasting cases, she argued, was not private ownership or outside control but a set of arrangements the users had worked out themselves. The boundaries of the resource and the list of people entitled to use it were clear. The people bound by the rules had a voice in changing them. Users monitored one another, and penalties for breaking the rules were graduated: a first offense might bring a small fine or a public warning, while repeated offenses brought heavier ones. Disputes could be settled quickly and cheaply, often by the users themselves.

Some of her findings ran against common sense. Rules imposed by distant authorities, however well designed, often worked worse than rougher rules that users had made, partly because outsiders could not watch every field and canal, and partly because people who had no say in a rule had less reason to respect it. In several cases, a government that took over a well-run commons with good intentions destroyed the very cooperation it meant to protect.

In 2009 Ostrom became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in economics. Her work did not prove Hardin wrong so much as show that he had described one possible ending as if it were the only one. The herders in his story never speak to one another. Ostrom's herders do, and that difference turns out to matter a great deal.

passages.title: What the Horn Heard
passages.text:
When people listen to the earliest recordings of music, made in the decades around 1900, they often assume they are hearing how the musicians of that era sounded. The assumption is understandable. A recording seems to be a kind of window: the performer played, the machine listened, and the result was preserved. But the machines of that period did not listen the way a person in a concert hall did, and the musicians who made records knew it. What survives is less a window than a negotiation between players and a device with strong preferences of its own.

Before about 1925, records were made acoustically. There was no microphone and no electrical amplifier. Musicians played or sang into the wide mouth of a large horn, which funneled the sound onto a thin diaphragm. The diaphragm vibrated, and a stylus attached to it cut a wavering groove into a slowly turning disc of soft wax. Everything depended on the energy of the sound itself. A loud, focused tone pushed the diaphragm hard and cut a clear groove; a soft or scattered one barely moved it.

The horn's preferences shaped the music in ways that a listener today can easily miss. Very low notes registered poorly, so the deep pulse of a string bass often vanished from the groove. Recording directors commonly replaced it with a tuba, whose blunter tone carried better. Violins, whose sound spreads in many directions, were sometimes swapped for an odd hybrid instrument that sent the strings' vibration through a metal horn of its own, aimed straight at the recording horn. Pianos were pushed close and raised on blocks. Singers with gentle voices were told to project as though addressing the back row of a theater, and to step back from the horn on their loudest notes so that they would not overload the groove.

Time was limited as well. A ten-inch disc turning at roughly seventy-eight revolutions per minute held about three minutes of music on a side. A popular song could be trimmed to fit, but a longer work could not simply be played as written. Symphonies were divided into segments, and the performers had to stop, wait for a fresh wax blank, and begin again, sometimes at a tempo a little quicker than they would have chosen in a concert, so that a movement would fit on as few sides as possible.

None of this means that early records are worthless as evidence. They preserve real details of phrasing, ornament, and pronunciation that no written score could capture, and historians of performance study them closely. But they must be read the way one reads any document produced under unusual conditions: with attention to what the conditions encouraged and what they made impossible. A forceful delivery on a disc from 1910 may tell us less about the singer's taste than about the horn the singer was standing in front of.

When electrical recording arrived, with microphones and amplifiers, the negotiation changed its terms. A microphone could catch a quiet voice from a short distance, and a new, intimate style of popular singing, soft and conversational, became possible almost at once. It is tempting to say that the technology simply freed performers to sound like themselves. Yet microphones had preferences too. They rewarded a different kind of singer, and some voices that had thrived in front of the horn sounded harsh or thin up close. Each new device, it seems, did not remove the go-between standing between performer and listener. It replaced one go-between with another, and musicians, as they always had, learned to play to it.

candidates.subskill: Central claim of a research narrative
candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Shared resources are always ruined in the end unless they are divided up into private property.
choices.B: Governments generally manage shared resources more fairly than the people who actually use them.
choices.C: Village herders in Switzerland have shared their summer pastures for many centuries.
choices.D: Field studies showed that the users of a shared resource can sometimes avoid the ruin one theory predicted.

candidates.evidence: Her point was that collapse is not inevitable.
candidates.explanation: The passage presents Hardin's prediction and then Ostrom's evidence that communities sometimes managed shared resources well, showing collapse is not inevitable.

A.rationale: This is Hardin's conclusion, which the passage says Ostrom's cases qualified.

B.rationale: Paragraph 5 says outside control often worked worse.

C.rationale: This is one example from paragraph 3, not the main idea.

hints: What does Ostrom show about Hardin's prediction?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the conflict between the two views.

candidates.remember: The main idea usually resolves the passage's central disagreement.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Hardin concluded that shared resources would be destroyed unless they were:

choices.A: split into private holdings or put under government control.
choices.B: managed by rules the users had made for themselves.
choices.C: limited to a few herders who knew one another well.
choices.D: studied carefully by economists before any rules were set.

candidates.evidence: unless they were either divided into private property or placed under the control of a government
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says Hardin concluded that shared resources would be destroyed unless divided into private property or placed under government control.

B.rationale: This is Ostrom's finding, not Hardin's conclusion.

C.rationale: Hardin's essay as described says nothing about the number of herders.

D.rationale: The passage says economists applied Hardin's idea, not that he called for study.

hints: Find the last sentence of paragraph 1.
candidates.remember: Keep track of whose view each claim belongs to.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of paragraph 2 is to:

choices.A: present evidence that Hardin's idea correctly explained overfishing.
choices.B: show how widely Hardin's idea was accepted before anyone tested it closely.
choices.C: introduce the research methods that Ostrom later used.
choices.D: criticize economists for ignoring problems such as polluted rivers.

candidates.evidence: For years many economists treated the tragedy less as a hypothesis to be tested than as a law to be applied.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the argument spread quickly and was treated as a law rather than a hypothesis, setting up Ostrom's decision to test it.

A.rationale: The paragraph says the idea seemed to explain overfishing, not that evidence confirmed it.

C.rationale: Ostrom's methods are introduced in paragraph 3.

D.rationale: The paragraph says economists applied the idea to such problems, not that they ignored them.

hints: How does paragraph 2 prepare for paragraph 3?

strategy.explanation: Ask what problem paragraph 3 responds to.

candidates.remember: A short paragraph often sets up the next one.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word graduated most nearly means:

choices.A: having finished a course of study.
choices.D: applied the same way to everyone.

candidates.evidence: a first offense might bring a small fine or a public warning, while repeated offenses brought heavier ones
candidates.explanation: The example that follows shows penalties starting small and growing heavier with repeated offenses, so graduated means increasing in steps.

A.rationale: This is the common meaning, which does not fit penalties.

B.rationale: This meaning fits a measuring cup, not a set of penalties.

D.rationale: The passage stresses that penalties grew with repeated offenses, not that they were uniform.

strategy.explanation: Use the example after the colon.

candidates.remember: An example right after a word often defines it.

candidates.subskill: Inference about why outside rules failed
candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 5, rules imposed by distant authorities often worked worse than rules made by users partly because the distant authorities:

choices.A: could not observe how the resource was actually being used day to day.
choices.B: designed rules that were more lenient than the users' own rules.
choices.C: lacked the money needed to enforce penalties on users.
choices.D: intended to take control of the resource away from the users.

candidates.evidence: partly because outsiders could not watch every field and canal
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 gives two reasons: outsiders could not watch every field and canal, and users had less reason to respect rules they had no say in. A matches the first.

B.rationale: The paragraph says imposed rules could be well designed; leniency is not mentioned.

C.rationale: Cost of enforcement is not given as a reason.

D.rationale: The paragraph says some governments acted with good intentions.

hints: Paragraph 5 gives two reasons; find them.

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence that begins 'Rules imposed by distant authorities.'

candidates.remember: Look for 'partly because' to find stated reasons.

candidates.subskill: Function of examples within an argument
candidates.stem: The examples of the Swiss pastures and the Spanish irrigation canals in paragraph 3 mainly serve to:

choices.A: prove that every shared resource can be managed well by its users.
choices.B: show that European farmers were more cooperative than farmers elsewhere.
choices.C: illustrate Hardin's argument that shared pastures are soon overgrazed.
choices.D: give real cases in which a shared resource lasted under rules its users enforced.

candidates.evidence: under rules that limited how many animals each family could send up the mountain
candidates.explanation: Both examples describe commons that lasted for centuries or generations under rules users enforced themselves, giving real counterexamples to Hardin's imagined pasture.

A.rationale: Paragraph 4 says many of Ostrom's cases ended in collapse.

B.rationale: The passage makes no comparison between regions.

C.rationale: The examples are of commons that lasted, which is the opposite of Hardin's prediction.

hints: Do the examples support Hardin or challenge him?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the examples have in common.

candidates.remember: Examples support the claim around them; check which claim.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must see the examples as counterexamples while avoiding the overstatement that every commons succeeds, which paragraph 4 rules out.

candidates.subskill: Author's view of an earlier argument
candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the author's view of Hardin's argument, as expressed in the last paragraph?

choices.A: It described one real outcome but wrongly treated that outcome as the only possible one.
choices.B: It was mistaken about every one of the shared resources that Ostrom later studied.
choices.C: It was correct, and Ostrom's research merely added further supporting examples to it.
choices.D: It was too abstract to say anything useful about real pastures or fisheries.

candidates.evidence: Her work did not prove Hardin wrong so much as show that he had described one possible ending as if it were the only one.
candidates.explanation: The last paragraph says Ostrom did not prove Hardin wrong so much as show he had described one possible ending as if it were the only one.

B.rationale: Paragraph 4 says many of Ostrom's cases did collapse, as Hardin predicted.

C.rationale: The author says Ostrom showed collapse is not inevitable, which Hardin denied.

D.rationale: The author calls it elegant and says it described a real possible ending.

hints: What does 'not ... so much as' tell you about the author's view?

strategy.explanation: Read the second sentence of the last paragraph.

candidates.remember: 'Not X so much as Y' signals a partial agreement.

author_checklist.hardness: The author partly agrees and partly disagrees; both the 'mistaken' and 'correct' choices catch readers who miss the qualification.

candidates.stem: The author's statement that "The herders in his story never speak to one another" (last paragraph) most strongly suggests that Hardin's model left out:

choices.A: the damage that extra animals do to a shared pasture.
choices.B: the ability of users to agree on and enforce shared rules.
choices.C: the role of governments in dividing land among herders.
choices.D: the benefit each herder gains from adding one more animal.

candidates.evidence: Ostrom's herders do, and that difference turns out to matter a great deal.
candidates.explanation: Ostrom's lasting cases depended on users making, monitoring and enforcing rules together (paragraph 4). Herders who never speak cannot do that, so the remark points to what Hardin left out.

A.rationale: Hardin's story includes this damage explicitly.

C.rationale: Hardin did include government control as one solution.

D.rationale: This benefit is the core of Hardin's story.

hints: What did Ostrom's lasting cases have that requires talking?

strategy.explanation: Connect the last paragraph to paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: Interpret a figurative remark using the rest of the passage.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must link a figurative remark in the last paragraph to the arrangements described in paragraph 4.

candidates.subskill: Applying the findings to a new case
candidates.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following arrangements for a shared community well would Ostrom most likely expect to last?

choices.A: A distant agency sets detailed rules and sends an inspector to the well once each year.
choices.B: Each household may draw as much water as it likes, and no one ever checks how much is taken.
choices.C: Neighbors set and revise the rules, take turns checking the well, and raise fines for repeat offenses.
choices.D: A single household buys the well and sells water to neighbors at whatever price it chooses.

candidates.evidence: The people bound by the rules had a voice in changing them.
candidates.explanation: The key matches the arrangements paragraph 4 lists for lasting commons: users make and change the rules, monitor one another and use graduated penalties.

A.rationale: Paragraph 5 says distant rules that outsiders cannot watch often fail.

B.rationale: This is the open-access situation Hardin warned about.

D.rationale: Ostrom found lasting cases without private ownership; this is Hardin's privatization remedy.

hints: List the features paragraph 4 gives for lasting cases.

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against those features.

candidates.remember: Apply the author's criteria to a new example.

candidates.subskill: Inference across paragraphs about which performers benefited
candidates.stem: Based on paragraphs 3 and 6, which singer would most likely have found it easier to record after microphones arrived than before?

choices.A: A singer whose gentle voice barely moved the diaphragm of a recording horn
choices.B: A singer whose forceful voice could fill a large theater without strain
choices.C: A singer who preferred songs that ran longer than three minutes
choices.D: A singer who had learned to step back from the horn on loud notes

candidates.evidence: A microphone could catch a quiet voice from a short distance
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says gentle voices had to be pushed to project for the horn, and paragraph 6 says a microphone could catch a quiet voice from a short distance, so a gentle-voiced singer gained the most.

B.rationale: Paragraph 6 suggests some voices that thrived in front of the horn sounded harsh up close.

C.rationale: The passage ties the three-minute limit to the disc, and nothing says microphones changed it.

D.rationale: Stepping back was a skill for the horn; the passage does not say it helped with microphones.

hints: What did gentle voices struggle with before 1925, and what changed with the microphone?

strategy.explanation: Combine the problem in paragraph 3 with the change in paragraph 6.

candidates.remember: Connect a problem in one paragraph with its solution in another.

revision_history.reason: The key paraphrased a single sentence, so the item was a locate-the-detail lookup despite inference framing; rebuilt as a two-paragraph inference on the same passage.
